argument:
The bear's distinction between activity growth and risk-adjusted return is correct. The supplied $16.9bn earnings excluding significant items nevertheless provides an earnings anchor after removing much of the headline-gain distortion. No matched prior-year adjusted comparison is supplied, so it should support continuing profitability rather than a claimed adjusted growth rate.

A conditional bank buy case combines that operating earnings base with capital, liquidity, funding and asset-quality verification. The $2.5bn credit-cost figure cannot be called benign or adverse without the missing context. Loan growth creates opportunity and risk; deposit growth supplies activity evidence without proving funding costs. Neither 14.24x P/E nor oversold price action proves value. The bearish case establishes the required bank-specific gates without refuting the existence of sizeable earnings excluding special items.
key_points: Earnings excluding significant items provide an anchor, not adjusted YoY-growth proof.
Loan and deposit growth need risk-adjusted interpretation.
Credit, capital and liquidity checks determine purchase conviction.
rebuttal_to_previous: I agree franchise growth does not establish improved risk-adjusted returns. My narrower counterargument is that $16.9bn excluding significant items demonstrates substantial earnings independent of the headline gains. That preserves a conditional buy thesis pending the bank supplement, without treating the correction as a verified bargain.
